title: How Nuclear Fusion Could Power the Future

slides.heading: How Nuclear Fusion Could Power the Future
slides.body: The star-powered energy source that could change civilization forever

slides.heading: What Is Nuclear Fusion?
slides.body: Fusion is the process that powers the sun: two light atomic nuclei (like hydrogen isotopes) combine to form a heavier nucleus, releasing enormous energy. Unlike fission, it splits no heavy atoms — it fuses light ones together.

slides.heading: Why It's So Hard to Achieve
slides.body: Fusing nuclei requires overcoming their electric repulsion, which demands temperatures exceeding 100 million degrees Celsius — hotter than the sun's core. Containing that plasma without it touching any surface is an engineering challenge unlike any other.

slides.heading: The Fuel: Deuterium & Tritium
slides.body: The most viable fusion reaction uses deuterium and tritium — both hydrogen isotopes. Deuterium is extracted from seawater (virtually unlimited), and tritium can be bred from lithium. One bathtub of seawater holds the energy equivalent of 300 tonnes of coal.

slides.heading: Magnetic Confinement: Tokamaks
slides.body: The leading design uses doughnut-shaped devices called tokamaks that confine plasma with powerful magnetic fields. ITER, under construction in France, will be the world's largest tokamak — a global collaboration of 35 nations building the most complex machine ever made.

slides.heading: The 2022 NIF Breakthrough
slides.body: In December 2022, the National Ignition Facility in California achieved ignition — laser-driven fusion that produced more energy than the lasers delivered to the target. This landmark proved the physics works. It was the first time fusion energy exceeded input energy in a controlled experiment.

slides.heading: Private Sector Racing Ahead
slides.body: Companies like Commonwealth Fusion Systems, TAE Technologies, and Helion are betting billions that compact, high-field magnets and new designs can reach commercial fusion faster than government mega-projects. Helion has a Power Purchase Agreement with Microsoft for electricity by 2028.

slides.heading: Why Fusion Is Safer Than Fission
slides.body: Fusion produces no long-lived radioactive waste — only helium and short-lived activated materials. It cannot melt down: shut off the fuel and the reaction stops in seconds. There is no risk of a Chernobyl or Fukushima-style catastrophe.

slides.heading: The Remaining Engineering Challenges
slides.body: Achieving net energy gain at scale, developing materials that survive neutron bombardment for decades, and building a system that breeds enough tritium to sustain itself are the last major hurdles. Each is formidable — but none violates the laws of physics.

slides.heading: A Star on Earth
slides.body: If fusion succeeds, it promises abundant, clean energy for millennia with minimal waste and no carbon emissions. The question is no longer 'if' but 'when' — and the race to get there is on.
